Daniel frames the assignment as “six sketches of arbitrary content,” but the set isn’t arbitrary at all: it clusters around urban wayfinding (Route A signage, subway entrance), institutional authority (the “angry Varner” caricature), and small surreal ruptures (sword through ceramics, book in water, dream figure). That unacknowledged pattern matters because “visual communication” is less about rendering objects than about making a viewer infer priorities, relationships, and stakes. Even the most observational image here is already a claim about what deserves emphasis: the Route A drawing devotes disproportionate care to the typographic construction and framing of the sign, effectively treating lettering as subject, not label—very much in line with the Bauhaus-era idea that form and message are inseparable.

The blind spot is that Daniel doesn’t yet articulate what each sketch is trying to *do* to a viewer. Several drawings hint at distinct communicative modes—diagrammatic clarity (signage), narrative gag (subway “MINT” figure), symbolic tableau (book submerged), caricatural affect (Varner)—but without a sentence on intent, the reader can’t tell whether the unevenness in line weight, perspective, and background detail is a choice or a limitation. A simple rubric (“What is the message? Who is the audience? What should they notice first?”) would turn this post from a gallery into an argument, and it would also surface how these images oscillate between depiction and symbol—territory mapped crisply in [John Berger’s *Ways of Seeing*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ways_of_Seeing) and [Rudolf Arnheim’s *Art and Visual Perception*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_and_Visual_Perception). One practical extension: pick one sketch (say, the subway entrance) and redraw it twice—once optimized for legibility at a glance, once optimized for mood—because the difference between those versions is essentially the difference between “drawing” and “visual communication.”
